===Music===
The musician and instrument maker, [[Arnold Dolmetsch]], was born in France in 1858 and moved with his son, [[Carl Dolmetsch]] to Haslemere in 1919.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.haslemeresociety.org/arnold--carl-dolmetsch.html |title= Arnold and Carl Dolmetsch blue plaque |author= <!--Not stated--> |publisher= Haslemere Society |access-date= 14 November 2021 |archive-date= 4 November 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20211104140826/http://www.haslemeresociety.org/arnold--carl-dolmetsch.html |url-status= live }}</ref> The family repopularised the [[recorder (instrument)|recorder]] and began the revival of other [[early music|early musical instruments]]. In 1925, they launched the Haslemere Festival, which later became the annual International Dolmetsch Early Music Festival.<ref>{{cite news |last= Godwin |first= Sheilagh |date= 13 July 1997 |title= Obituary: Carl Dolmetsch |url= https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/obituary-carl-dolmetsch-1250692.html |work= The Independent |access-date= 31 October 2021 |archive-date= 31 October 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20211031181650/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/obituary-carl-dolmetsch-1250692.html |url-status= live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.haslemeresociety.org/arnold--carl-dolmetsch.html |title= Arnold and Carl Dolmetsch Blue Plaque |author= <!--Not stated--> |year= 2021 |publisher= Haslemere Society |access-date= 31 October 2021 |archive-date= 4 November 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20211104140826/http://www.haslemeresociety.org/arnold--carl-dolmetsch.html |url-status= live }}</ref> From 1997 to 2018, the director of the festival was Carl Dolmetsch's daughter, Jeanne-Marie Dolmetsch.<ref>{{cite news |author= <!--Not stated--> |date= 2 December 2018 |title= Tributes paid to early music revivalist Jeanne-Marie Dolmetsch |url= https://www.haslemereherald.com/article.cfm?id=131598&headline=Tributes+paid+to+early+music+revivalist+Jeanne-Marie+Dolmetsch&sectionIs=news&searchyear=2018 |work= Haslemere Herald |access-date= 14 November 2021 |archive-date= 14 November 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20211114211519/https://www.haslemereherald.com/article.cfm?id=131598&headline=Tributes+paid+to+early+music+revivalist+Jeanne-Marie+Dolmetsch&sectionIs=news&searchyear=2018 |url-status= live }}</ref>

Founded as the Haslemere Orchestral Society in 1923, the Haslemere Musical Society acquired its current name in 1939. Among its former conductors are [[Anthony Bernard]], the founder of the [[London Chamber Orchestra]],<ref>{{harvnb|Chandler|1973|p=91}}</ref><ref name=Music_Soc>{{cite web |url= https://www.hmsoc.org.uk/dbpage.php?pg=history |title= History |last= Sharpe |first= Peter |date= 20 July 2020 |publisher= Haslemere Musical Society |access-date= 20 October 2021 |archive-date= 20 October 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20211020170206/https://www.hmsoc.org.uk/dbpage.php?pg=history |url-status= live }}</ref> the composer [[John Gardner (composer)|John Gardner]] and [[John Lubbock (conductor)|John Lubbock]], founder of the [[Orchestra of St John's|Orchestra of St John's Smith Square]]. In 2007, the society commissioned the choral work ''Lord of All Creation'' by outgoing conductor, Darrell Davison. The current conductor is [[James Ross (conductor)|James Ross]]. The society gives regular concerts in the local area and holds an annual "come and sing" event.<ref name=Music_Soc/>

Haslemere Town Band was officially founded in 1837 following the amalgamation of two small bands which had started in 1834.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.farnhamherald.com/article.cfm?id=114858&headline=Museum%20has%20a%20new%20acquisition&sectionIs=news&searchyear=2016|title=Museum has a new acquisition|date=23 November 2016|newspaper=Farnham Herald|access-date=19 September 2021|archive-date=20 September 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210920213005/https://www.farnhamherald.com/article.cfm?id=114858&headline=Museum%20has%20a%20new%20acquisition&sectionIs=news&searchyear=2016|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Haslemere Educational Museum===
{{main|Haslemere Educational Museum}}
Haslemere Educational Museum was founded in 1888 by the surgeon, [[Jonathan Hutchinson]], who was an amateur collector of biological, geological and anthropological specimens. Initially the museum was located at Hutchinson's Haslemere home, Inval, but moved to its current location on the High Street in 1926. In the same year, it acquired a collection of European Folk Art from the Peasant Arts Museum, which had been located in the town.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.haslemeremuseum.co.uk/about.html |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210918022644/https://www.haslemeremuseum.co.uk/about.html |archive-date=18 September 2021 |title= About us |author=<!--Not stated--> |year= 2021 |publisher= Haslemere Educational Museum |access-date= 17 September 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.haslemeremuseum.co.uk/collections/des/peasant-arts/Peasant-Arts-Collection.html |title= "For love not money" Haslemere Peasant Art |last= Davies |first= G.S. |year= 2021 |publisher= Haslemere Museum |access-date= 27 October 2021 |archive-date= 8 April 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180408125324/http://www.haslemeremuseum.co.uk/collections/des/peasant-arts/Peasant-Arts-Collection.html |url-status= live }}</ref>

===Replica Penfold pillar box===
[[File:Penfold post box, Haslemere - geograph.org.uk - 1044643.jpg|thumb|upright|right|Penfold pillar box]]
A [[replica]] Victorian [[pillar box]] was installed outside the Georgian Hotel on the High Street in July 1992. ===Town Hall===
[[File:Haslemere town hall and war memorial.jpg|thumb|right|[[Haslemere Town Hall]] and war memorial]]
[[Haslemere Town Hall]], at the south end of the High Street, was constructed in 1814. Originally a [[market house]], it replaced an older wooden building, that had stood immediately to the north.<ref name=Rolston_1978a_p77/><ref name=Rolston_1978a_p88/> It was transferred to the Parish Council in 1897<ref>{{harvnb|Rolston|1978a|p=97}}</ref> and the upper floor was used as the debating chamber until 1926, when the UDC moved to the former museum building.<ref name=Rolston_1978b_p79/>

===War memorials===
The limestone war memorial in Haslemere High Street, was designed by [[Inigo Triggs]] in 1920–21. It takes the form of a gabled stone cross, supported on an octagonal column, which in turn rests on a stepped stone base.<ref>{{NHLE|num=1390566|desc=War Memorial, The Green|grade=II|fewer-links=yes}}</ref> It commemorates 62 local residents who died in WWI, whose names are inscribed on the plinth. The surnames of 47 people who died in the WWII are listed on bronze plaques.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.iwm.org.uk/memorials/item/memorial/23646 |title= Haslemere: Cross |author= <!--Not stated--> |year= 2017 |publisher= Imperial War Museum |access-date= 17 September 2021 |archive-date= 17 September 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210917201127/https://www.iwm.org.uk/memorials/item/memorial/23646 |url-status= live }}</ref> A restoration project, undertaken in 2018, included the repair and replacement of damaged stonework and was partly funded by the [[War Memorials Trust]].<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.warmemorials.org/search-grants/?gID=563 |title= Haslemere |author= <!--Not stated--> |publisher= War Memorials Trust |access-date= 17 September 2021 |archive-date= 6 April 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160406180010/http://www.warmemorials.org/search-grants/?gID=563 |url-status= live }}</ref>

The Grayswood war memorial is to the south of the village, on the west side of the A286. It takes the form of a freestanding stone cross and the base is inscribed with the words "Peace to those who died that we might live". It commemorates 19 local residents who died in WWI and three residents who died in WWII.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.iwm.org.uk/memorials/item/memorial/23636 |title= Grayswood: Cross |author= <!--Not stated--> |year= 2017 |publisher= Imperial War Museum |access-date= 18 November 2021 |archive-date= 18 November 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20211118173948/https://www.iwm.org.uk/memorials/item/memorial/23636 |url-status= live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.warmemorialsonline.org.uk/memorial/259923/ |title= Grayswood war memorial |author= <!--Not stated--> |orig-date= 28 September 2018 |date= 16 September 2019 |publisher= War Memorials Online |access-date= 18 November 2021 |archive-date= 18 November 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20211118173951/https://www.warmemorialsonline.org.uk/memorial/259923/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

==Parks and open spaces==
===Grayswood===
The [[National Trust]] owns a {{convert|4.17|ha|acre|abbr=on|adj=on}} area of mature oak and yew woodland between Grayswood village and Haslemere.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/visiting-woods/woods/grayswood/ |title= Grayswood |author= <!--Not stated--> |year= 2021 |publisher= Woodland Trust |access-date= 18 September 2021 |archive-date= 1 December 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20201201031641/https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/visiting-woods/woods/grayswood/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

===Grayswood Common, St George's Wood===
Grayswood Common and St George's Wood are located between Grayswood village and Haslemere and have a combined area of {{convert|16.43|ha|acre|abbr=on}}.<ref name=WT_Grayswood>{{cite web |url= https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/visiting-woods/woods/grayswood-common-and-st-georges-wood/ |title= Grayswood Common and St George's Wood |author= <!--Not stated--> |year= 2021 |publisher= Woodland Trust |access-date= 18 September 2021 |archive-date= 1 December 2020 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20201201023137/https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/visiting-woods/woods/grayswood-common-and-st-georges-wood/ |url-status= live }}</ref> They were acquired by the Urban District Council (UDC) in 1953<ref>{{harvnb|Rolston|1978b|p=99}}</ref> and are now owned by Waverley Borough Council.<ref name=WT_Grayswood/>

===Haste Hill===
Haste Hill is a {{convert|12.25|ha|acre|0|adj=on|abbr=on}} woodland to the south east of the town, owned by Waverley Borough Council.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/visiting-woods/woods/haste-hill-common/ |title= Haste Hill Common |author= <!--Not stated--> |year= 2021 |publisher= Woodland Trust |access-date= 21 October 2021 |archive-date= 18 January 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210118043033/https://www.woodlandtrust.org.uk/visiting-woods/woods/haste-hill-common/ |url-status= live }}</ref> There was a [[tenement]] on the hill in the 14th century and it may have been the site of the original settlement of Haslemere.<ref name=Malden_1911_pp45-49/> In the early 18th century, an [[optical telegraph]] station, part of the [[Admiralty (United Kingdom)|Admiralty]] Semaphore line between London and [[HMNB Portsmouth|Portsmouth]] was constructed on Haste Hill. It operated from 1822 until 1847, when it was superseded by an [[electrical telegraph]] line between the two cities.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.exploringsurreyspast.org.uk/surreys-semaphore-stations/ |title= Signal the fleet! Surrey's Semaphore Stations |author= <!--Not stated--> |date= 1 May 2019 |orig-date= 13 February 2017 |publisher= Exploring Surrey's Past |access-date= 21 October 2021 |archive-date= 22 June 2017 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20170622164605/http://www.exploringsurreyspast.org.uk/surreys-semaphore-stations/ |url-status= live }}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Swanton|Woods|1914|pp=228–230}}</ref>

===Lion Green===
[[File:Lion Green, Shottermill, Haslemere (Nov 2021).jpg|thumb|Lion Green]]

Lion Green was designated a recreation ground and open space in the [[Inclosure Act 1845]].<ref name=Rolston_1978b_p70/> The green is used for several community events including the annual Haslemere Classic Car Festival and the biennial Haslemere Fringe Festival.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://haslemeretc.org/service/hiring-lion-green/ |title= Hiring Lion Green |author= <!--Not stated--> |date= 11 June 2021 |publisher= Haslemere Town Council |access-date= 18 November 2021 |archive-date= 18 November 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20211118171758/https://haslemeretc.org/service/hiring-lion-green/ |url-status= live }}</ref>

===Recreation ground===
The {{convert|3.44|ha|acre|adj=on|abbr=on}} recreation ground adjoins Scotland Lane and Old Haslemere Road.<ref name=FiT_Rec>{{cite web |url= https://www.fieldsintrust.org/FieldSite/Haslemere-Recreation-Ground |title= Haslemere Recreation Ground |author= <!--Not stated--> |year= 2021 |publisher= Fields in Trust |access-date= 20 September 2021 |archive-date= 16 October 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20211016162002/https://www.fieldsintrust.org/FieldSite/Haslemere-Recreation-Ground |url-status= live }}</ref> The land was purchased in 1921 by the War Memorial Committee, using surplus funds donated for the construction of the memorial in the High Street.<ref name=Rolston_1978b_p70/> It was presented to the UDC in the same year, in memory of those who had died in the First World War.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.roll-of-honour.com/Surrey/Haslemere.html |title= Haslemere War Memorial |last= Jeffers |first= Barbara |year= 2006 |publisher= Roll of Honour |access-date= 18 September 2021 |archive-date= 3 March 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160303192550/http://www.roll-of-honour.com/Surrey/Haslemere.html |url-status= live }}</ref> In 2015, the recreation ground was legally protected by the charity, [[Fields in Trust]], and was designated a Queen Elizabeth II field.<ref name=FiT_Rec/>

===Swan Barn Farm===
[[File:Footpath through Swan Barn Farm, Haslemere (geograph 4164045).jpg|thumb|right|Entrance to Swan Barn Farm]]
Swan Barn Farm, owned by the National Trust, is an area of grassland and ancient woodland to the east of Haslemere High Street. The {{convert|28|ha|acre|abbr=on|adj=on}} property includes two [[orchard]]s and is run as a [[smallholding]]. Areas of [[pasture]] are mown for [[hay]]making and are also [[conservation grazing|grazed]] by [[Belted Galloway]] cattle. The Hunter Base Camp, which provides accommodation for long-term volunteers working on Blackdown, is part of the farm.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.haslemere-nt.com/sb.html |title= Swan Barn Farm |author= <!--Not stated--> |year= 2014 |publisher= Black Down & Hindhead Supporters of the National Trust |access-date= 18 September 2021 |archive-date= 21 February 2018 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20180221073422/http://www.haslemere-nt.com/sb.html |url-status= live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/swan-barn-farm |year= 2021 |title= Swan Barn Farm |author= <!--Not stated--> |publisher= National Trust |access-date= 18 September 2021 |archive-date= 30 July 2021 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20210730122901/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/swan-barn-farm |url-status= live }}</ref>

1008009.title: Petworth House
1008009.extract:
Petworth House is a late 17th-century Grade I listed country house in the parish of Petworth, West Sussex, England. It was built in 1688 by Charles Seymour, 6th Duke of Somerset, and altered in the 1870s to the design of the architect Anthony Salvin. It contains intricate wood-carvings by Grinling Gibbons (d. 1721). It is the manor house of the manor of Petworth. For centuries it was the southern home for the Percy family, earls of Northumberland.
Petworth is famous for its extensive art collection made by the Northumberland and Seymour/Somerset families and George Wyndham, 3rd Earl of Egremont (1751–1837), containing many works by his friend J. M. W. Turner. It also has an expansive deer park, landscaped by Capability Brown, which contains a large herd of fallow deer.

[[File:Percy (4 quarters) impaling Poynings (4 quarters), Percy Window, Petworth House.jpg|thumb|The 16th-century Percy Window in [[Petworth House Chapel]], showing the arms of Henry Percy, 3rd Earl of Northumberland (1421–1461) [[impalement (heraldry)|impaled]] with the arms of Eleanor Poynings, his wife]]
[[File:Benjamin Robert Haydon (1786-1846) - Alexander the Great (356–323 BC), Taming Bucephalus - 485149 - National Trust.jpg|thumb|200px|[[Benjamin Robert Haydon]] 1826 painting ''Alexander the Great Taming Bucephalus'' painted for Petworth House]] 
'''Petworth House''' is a late 17th-century Grade I listed [[English country house|country house]] in the parish of [[Petworth]], [[West Sussex]], [[England]]. It was built in 1688 by [[Charles Seymour, 6th Duke of Somerset]], and altered in the 1870s to the design of the architect [[Anthony Salvin]].<ref>{{National Heritage List for England|num=1225989|desc=Petworth House|access-date=12 November 2014}}</ref> It contains intricate wood-carvings by [[Grinling Gibbons]] (d. 1721). It is the [[manor house]] of the [[Manorialism|manor]] of Petworth. For centuries it was the southern home for the [[House of Percy|Percy family]], [[Earl of Northumberland|earls of Northumberland]].

Petworth is famous for its extensive art collection made by the Northumberland and Seymour/Somerset families and [[George Wyndham, 3rd Earl of Egremont]] (1751–1837), containing many works by his friend [[J. M. W. Turner]]. It also has an expansive [[Deer park (England)|deer park]], landscaped by [[Capability Brown]], which contains a large herd of [[fallow deer]].

==History==

===Medieval manor house===
The manor of Petworth first came into the possession of the Percy family as a royal gift from [[Adeliza of Louvain]], the widow of King [[Henry I of England|Henry I]] (1100–1135), to her brother [[Joscelin of Louvain]].<ref name="nattrust">{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/petworth-house-and-park/features/manor-house-to-mansion-a-history-of-petworth|title=Petworth House and Park: History |publisher= [[National Trust]] |access-date=23 July 2021 }}</ref> He later married the Percy heiress and adopted the surname Percy. His descendants became the earls of Northumberland, the most powerful family in northern England. The Percy family, whose primary seat was at [[Alnwick Castle]] in Northumberland, bordering Scotland, intended Petworth to be for their occasional residence only.

The site was previously occupied by a fortified manor house built by [[Henry de Percy, 1st Baron Percy]] (1273–1314), in 1308–09, the chapel and [[undercroft]] of which still survive as part of the current house.<ref name="nattrust"/>

However, in the 16th century, the Percy family came into conflict with the crown as the staunchly Catholic family fell foul of the [[English Reformation]] which resulted in Petworth being briefly taken from them by King [[Henry VIII]], restored to them by Queen [[Mary I]] before the wider family came under scrutiny during the reign of Queen [[Elizabeth I]]. [[Thomas Percy, 7th Earl of Northumberland]], allied the family to [[Mary, Queen of Scots]], and led the 1569 [[Rising of the North]] against Elizabeth with the aim of deposing her and placing Mary on the throne – this failed and led to his execution for treason in 1572. His younger brother, [[Henry Percy, 8th Earl of Northumberland]], would regain his title from the Queen after begging her mercy and was granted his freedom on the condition that the family be confined to Petworth where they could be observed by the court. The house at Petworth was therefore transformed and expanded to become the permanent home of the family with grand stables erected and a pleasure garden laid out at this time.<ref name="nattrust"/><ref name=dommett2015>{{ cite journal | last=Dommett | first=Tom | date=2015 | title=Petworth Park's hidden past | journal=Sussex Archaeological Collections | volume=153 | pages=83–112 | doi=10.5284/1085964 | doi-access=free }}</ref> A part of this era manor house, a 'Lost' North wing, was discovered during archaeological excavations in 2012–15 under the lawn at the front of the house having been demolished in 1692.<ref name="nattrust"/><ref name=dommett2015/>

===Baroque house===
In 1670 [[Josceline Percy, 11th Earl of Northumberland]] (1644–1670), died without a male heir, and thus his considerable fortune and estates of Petworth House, Alnwick Castle, [[Syon House]] and [[Northumberland House]] were inherited by his 2-year-old daughter and sole heiress, Lady [[Elizabeth Seymour, Duchess of Somerset|Elizabeth Percy]] (1667–1722). In 1682, at the age of 16 and already twice widowed, she married the 20-year-old [[Charles Seymour, 6th Duke of Somerset]] (1662–1748), whose family seat was [[Marlborough Castle]] in Wiltshire. They became one of the wealthiest couples in England.<ref name="nattrust"/>

It was the 6th Duke, nicknamed 'the Proud Duke', and the Duchess who rebuilt the house between 1688 and 1702 in the [[Baroque architecture|Baroque]] style that favoured order and symmetry.<ref name="Nattrust family tree">{{cite web |title=The Petworth family tree |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/petworth-house-and-park/features/the-petworth-family-tree- |publisher= [[National Trust]] |access-date=23 July 2021}}</ref> It was very much inspired by the [[Palace of Versailles]] and aimed to establish Petworth as a rival to these European palaces.<ref name="nattrust"/>{{efn|"In 1682 Petworth passed by marriage from the Percies to the 6th Duke of Somerset and it is to him ''the Proud Duke'' that we owe by far the larger part of the existing house."<ref>{{ cite book | last=Nicolson | first=Nigel | date=1978 | title=The National Trust Book of Great Houses of Britain | location=London | publisher=Granada | isbn=978-0-586-05604-2 | page=165 }}</ref>}}

The grounds and wider parkland were also managed at this time with the parkland being home to quarries and proving an industrial and working landscape supporting the building works and the house. Around the house were planted more formal gardens including an avenue of [[Tilia|lime trees]] approaching the house, a canal gardens and fishponds, [[parterre]], great greenhouse and [[Orangery]]. Completing the formal gardens was a Quarter Piece Lawn and Rampart terraces comprising a series of walks carved into the hill and accompanied by carved seats, stairs and statues.<ref name=dommett2015/>

===Split inheritance challenges and Capability Brown===
Since 1750 the house and estate have been owned by the prominent [[Baron Leconfield|Wyndham]] family, descended from Sir [[Charles Wyndham, 2nd Earl of Egremont|Charles Wyndham, 4th Baronet]] (1710–1763), of [[Orchard Wyndham]] in Somerset, a nephew and co-heir of [[Algernon Seymour, 7th Duke of Somerset]] (1684–1750). As part of the inheritance and splitting-up of the great Percy inheritance, which had been a source of contention between the 7th Duke and his father the 6th Duke, in 1749<ref name="Debrett's Peerage 1968">Debrett's Peerage, 1968, p. 1037, ''Duke of Somerset''.</ref> after the death of the 6th Duke, King [[George II of Great Britain|George II]] granted the 7th Duke four extra titles in the [[peerage]], including Baron Cockermouth and [[Earl of Egremont]], with the latter two created with special remainder to Sir Charles Wyndham,<ref name="Debrett's Peerage 1968"/> the intended and actual recipient of Petworth, [[Cockermouth Castle]] and [[Egremont Castle]]. Following the 7th Duke's death in 1750, his lands and titles were split between his daughter, Lady [[Elizabeth Percy, Duchess of Northumberland (1716–1776)|Elizabeth Seymour]] and her husband Sir [[Hugh Percy, 1st Duke of Northumberland|Hugh Smithson, 4th Baronet]] (d.1786), and Charles Wyndham through the 7th Duke's deceased brother-in-law Sir [[Sir William Wyndham, 3rd Baronet|William Wyndham]]. The former inherited the northern Percy estates, including [[Alnwick Castle]] and [[Syon House]], together with the titles Baron Warkworth of [[Warkworth Castle]] and Earl of Northumberland<ref name="Debrett's Peerage 1968"/> and whose descendants are the current Dukes of Northumberland based at Alnwick Castle. The latter inherited Petworth and some estates in Sussex, Cumbria and Yorkshire as earls of Egremont.<ref name="Nattrust family tree"/>

The 2nd Earl was responsible for the collections of [[Rococo]] mirrors and antique statues that exist in the house today<ref>{{cite book |last1=Garnett |first1=Oliver |last2=Owen |first2=Diana |title=Petworth: A souvenir guide |date=2006 |publisher=The National Trust |location=Swindon |isbn=9781843592228 |page=2}}</ref> and was responsible for commissioning [[Capability Brown|Lancelot 'Capability' Brown]] to landscape the parkland during the 1750s and 1760s.<ref name="nattrust"/> The works involved the demolition of the formal gardens that preceded it, the landscaping of the wider parkland to raise the profile of the lawn in front of the house, infill quarries, smooth over the terraced walks and digging out buildings in the parkland down to foundation level. Archaeological investigations seemed to suggest that the turf was removed prior to the levelling works so they could be replaced after the works were completed and aiding the current natural look to the landscape.<ref name=dommett2015/>

===House of art===
It was [[George Wyndham, 3rd Earl of Egremont]] (1751–1837), who solidified the house's reputation as one of fine art. He inherited the house in 1763 and began what has been termed a "golden age" of Petworth when he expanded his collection of contemporary art and expanded and changed the house in order to display it best, in particular through the addition of the North Gallery in 1824–5.<ref name="Trust guide p16">{{cite book |last1=Garnett |first1=Oliver |last2=Owen |first2=Diana |title=Petworth: A souvenir guide |date=2006 |publisher=The National Trust |location=Swindon |isbn=9781843592228 |page=16}}</ref> He was patron to many contemporary artists including [[J. M. W. Turner]] and [[John Constable]] who were frequent guests to the house and painted the house and its parkland frequently - this has more recently helped inform restorations to the house and parkland.<ref name="Trust guide p16"/><ref name="Nattrust family tree"/>

The 3rd Earl bequeathed Petworth and Cockermouth Castle to his illegitimate son and adopted heir [[George Wyndham, 1st Baron Leconfield|Col. George Wyndham]] (1787–1869), but who could not inherit the title of Earl of Egremont so was instead created [[Baron Leconfield]] by [[Queen Victoria]] in 1859.

The title of Earl of Egremont instead passed to his nephew [[George Wyndham, 4th Earl of Egremont]] (1786–1845), who, while not inheriting Petworth, instead received the (not inconsiderable) [[entail]]ed Wyndham estates including [[Orchard Wyndham]] (still owned today by a Wyndham heir, William Wadham Wyndham, born 1940). The 4th Earl attempted to make up for the loss of Petworth by building his own stately home in Devon called [[Silverton Park]], which was demolished in 1902.

===Open to public: National Trust===
The house and deer park were handed over to the nation in 1947 by [[Charles Wyndham, 3rd Baron Leconfield]] (1872–1952), and are now managed by the [[National Trust]] under the name Petworth House & Park.<ref name="nattrust"/> The Leconfield Estates would continue to own much of Petworth and the surrounding area and the family would be able to continue living in part of Petworth House. It was [[John Wyndham, 1st Baron Egremont|John Wyndham]], 6th Baron Leconfield and since 1963 also 1st Baron Egremont,<ref name="Nattrust family tree"/> who negotiated the gift of the contents of the house, in particular the paintings and sculptures, into the property of the National Trust [[Acceptance in lieu|in lieu]] of accumulated death duties. The current Lord and Lady Egremont continue a tradition of unbroken occupancy at Petworth House today with [[Max Egremont]] and his family living in the south wing, allowing much of the remainder of the House to be open to the public.<ref name="Nattrust family tree"/> Lady Egremont has restored the gardens.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Lane Fox|first1=Robin|title=The countess who gave Petworth House its garden|url=https://www.ft.com/content/43b13490-fd1d-11e3-8ca9-00144feab7de|work=Financial Times}}</ref> In its 2018/2019 Annual Report, the Trust reported that Petworth House received 178,760 visitors.<ref>{{cite report| title=National Trust Annual Report 2018/19| publisher=National Trust| page=75| url=https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/documents/201819-annual-report.pdf| archive-date=29 February 2020| access-date=10 August 2022| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200229221120/https://nt.global.ssl.fastly.net/documents/201819-annual-report.pdf| url-status=dead}}</ref> In its 2022 Annual Report, the Trust reported that Petworth House received 147,079 visitors in 2021–22, having had a dip in numbers to 88,600 due to the [[COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom|COVID-19 pandemic]] in 2020–21.<ref>{{cite report | title=National Trust Annual Report 2022|publisher=National Trust | page=104 | url= https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/who-we-are/annual-reports }}</ref>

Today's building houses an important collection of paintings and sculptures, including 20 oil paintings by [[J. M. W. Turner]], who was a regular visitor to Petworth, paintings by [[Anthony van Dyck]] and [[Joshua Reynolds]], carvings by [[Grinling Gibbons]] and [[Ben Harms]], [[Classical sculpture|classical]]<ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.11141/ia.42.2 | issue=42 | title=Sanctioning Memory: Changing Identity. Using 3D laser scanning to identify two 'new' portraits of the Emperor Nero in English antiquarian collections | year=2016 | journal=Internet Archaeology | last1 = Russell | first1 = Miles| doi-access=free }}</ref> and [[neoclassical sculpture]]s (including ones by [[John Flaxman]] and [[John Edward Carew]]), and wall and ceiling paintings by [[Louis Laguerre]]. There is also a terrestrial [[globe]] by [[Emery Molyneux]], believed to be the only one in the world in its original 1592 state.<ref>{{cite web|title=Petworth House: Globe |url=http://www.yeoldesussexpages.com/petworth/norgal.htm |publisher=Ye Olde Sussex Pages |access-date=7 February 2008 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080808134827/http://www.yeoldesussexpages.com/petworth/norgal.htm |archive-date=8 August 2008 }}</ref>

==Petworth Park==
[[File:The Deer in Petworth Park by Joseph M. W. Turner 1827.jpeg|thumb|right|''The Deer in Petworth Park'', J. M. W. Turner, 1827.]]
The 283-hectare (700-acre) landscaped park, known as Petworth Park, contains a large herd of fallow deer.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/petworth-house/ |title=National Trust Petworth House and Park |work=web page |publisher=National Trust |access-date=20 April 2012}}</ref> It is one of the more famous in England, largely on account of a number of pictures of it which were painted by Turner. There is also a {{convert|12|ha|acre|adj=on}} [[woodland garden]], known as the Pleasure Ground<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.tourist-information-uk.com/petworth-house-and-park.htm |title=Petworth House and Park, Sussex |work=web page |publisher=Tourist Information UK |access-date=20 April 2012 |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120610015015/http://www.tourist-information-uk.com/petworth-house-and-park.htm |archive-date=10 June 2012 }}</ref> and some unusual [[ha-ha]]s.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.capabilitybrown.org/garden/petworth |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170621055010/http://www.capabilitybrown.org/garden/petworth |url-status=usurped |archive-date=21 June 2017 |title=Petworth |work=web page |publisher=Capability Brown 300 |access-date=30 December 2018}}</ref>
The landscaped park and pleasure grounds of Petworth are Grade I listed on the [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]].<ref>{{NHLE|num=1000162|desc=Petworth House|access-date=2 November 2017|mode=cs2}}</ref>

Petworth House is home to the Petworth House Real Tennis Club (many such private estates held [[real tennis]] courts). [[Petworth Park]] is also a cricket venue, for the refounded Petworth Park Cricket Club.

==Surrounding area==
As was usual for a mediaeval manor house, it was built in its original form next to the parish church (to provide the [[lord of the manor]] with enhanced spiritual benefits), around which developed a village, now grown to a sizeable town. Such position is unusual for a country mansion of its size and date, which were frequently later re-built on new more private sites away from the original manor house, or the church{{efn|As was the case for example at [[Castle Hill, Filleigh]], in Devon.}} and village were on occasion demolished to provide the desired privacy. Petworth House and Park are thus today situated immediately adjacent to the town of Petworth, with its shops and restaurants.

As an insight into the lives of past estate workers the [[Petworth Cottage Museum]] has been established in High Street, Petworth, furnished as it would have been in about 1910.

==Visitor facilities==
[[File:Restaurant in the great hall of the original Petworth House - geograph.org.uk - 237503.jpg|thumb|right|220px|Audit House Cafe at Petworth House.]]
Since being opened to the public, the house has attracted a significant number of visitors each year to see the art collections, explore the parkland and pleasure grounds. As such, the National Trust opened and run a number of facilities for visitors at the site.

The trust run two car parks for visitors, a main car park ideally placed for the house and pleasure gardens and a more northern car park for the wider deer park. With the exception of a visitor reception near to the main car park and a food and beverage kiosk in the old fire station, the visitor amenities are all located within the old service block for the house. This service wing contains the site shop, a second-hand bookshop,<ref name="Petworth NT shopping">{{cite web |title=Shopping at Petworth House |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/petworth-house-and-park/features/shopping-at-petworth-house |publisher=The National Trust |access-date=23 July 2021}}</ref> a cafe in the old Audit Room (which opened originally as a sculpture gallery before being used as a hall for large gatherings of the estate staff and servants),<ref>{{cite web |title=National Trust Petworth Audit Room Café |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/petworth-house-and-park/features/the-petworth-cafe |publisher=The National Trust |access-date=23 July 2021}}</ref> toilets and a seasonal art gallery. The service wing also contains a few of the historic kitchen rooms preserved for the public to view.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lewis |first1=Anna |title=Petworth house has re-opened - here are the new rules you need to know before your visit |url=https://www.sussexlive.co.uk/news/sussex-news/petworth-house-gardens-open-rules-4325038 |website=Sussex Live |publisher=Reach plc |access-date=23 July 2021 |date=14 July 2020}}</ref>

In addition to publishing a general visitor guidebook, the trust also publishes an in-depth guide to the different art pieces within the house and detailing in more detail the family history associated with the collection. They also have a virtual guide for visitors in addition to the volunteer room stewards present around the house.<ref>{{cite web |title=Petworth House downloadable house tour |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/petworth-house-and-park/features/petworth-house-downloadable-house-tour |publisher=The National Trust |access-date=23 July 2021}}</ref> They also announced in 2021 the opening of a second shop within the house selling books related to the art works in the house and art supplies.<ref name="Petworth NT shopping"/>

==Filming location==
[[File:Thomas Phillips (1770-1845) - The Allied Sovereigns at Petworth, 24 June 1814 (George, 1751–1837, 3rd Earl of Egremont, with His C - 486228 - National Trust.jpg|thumb|''[[The Allied Sovereigns at Petworth]]'' by [[Thomas Phillips]], 1817.]]
Petworth House has been used extensively as a location for film and TV productions. Included in the credits are ''[[Barry Lyndon]]'' (1975), ''[[Silver Bears]]'' (1977), ''[[Elizabeth: The Golden Age]]'' (2007), ''[[Maleficent (film)|Maleficent]]'' (2014), ''[[Mr Turner]]'' (2014),{{cn|date=September 2025}} ''[[Rebecca (2020 film)|Rebecca]]'' (2020),<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/discover/film-tv/explore-the-film-locations-of-rebecca|title=Explore the film locations of Rebecca|date=22 November 2022|website=[[National Trust]]}}</ref> and ''[[Bridgerton]]'' (2022).{{citation needed|date=April 2024}} ''[[Napoleon (2023 film)|Napoleon]]'', starring [[Joaquin Phoenix]] and [[Vanessa Kirby]] filmed at Petworth in March 2022.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sussexexpress.co.uk/people/west-sussex-landmark-features-in-ridley-scott-film-napoleon-featuring-joaquin-phoenix-and-vanessa-kirby-4231753|title=Ridley Scott film Napoleon featuring Joaquin Phoenix and Vanessa Kirby|date=25 July 2023|first=Joe|last=Stack|website=Sussex Express|access-date= 25 July 2023}}</ref>

'''Standen''' is an [[Arts and Crafts movement|Arts and Crafts]] house located to the south of [[East Grinstead]], West Sussex, England. The house and its surrounding gardens belong to the [[National Trust]] and are open to the public. It is a Grade I [[listed building]].<ref>{{National Heritage List for England |num=1249027 |desc=Standen |accessdate=16 November 2013 }}</ref>

==House==
[[Image:Standen Interior.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Interior of Standen]]

Between 1891 and 1894 [[architect]] [[Philip Webb]], who was a friend of [[William Morris]], designed the house for a prosperous [[London]] solicitor, James Beale, his wife Margaret, and their family of seven children. The house is constructed in the [[Weald]]en vernacular style with sandstone quarried from the estate and locally made bricks and tiles.<ref name=NT>{{cite book|last1=Garnett|first1=Oliver|title=Standen|date=2007|publisher=National Trust|location=Swindon|isbn=978-1-84359-286-0|page=2}}</ref> The interior is decorated with Morris carpets, fabrics and wallpapers, with furnishings also by Morris, and the garden complements the beauty of the house. From the start the house had electric power, originally generated by a donkey engine in a shed by the old barn.<ref name=NT /> The house still has its original electric light fittings, designed by [[William Arthur Smith Benson]].<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/standen-house-and-garden/features/a-history-of-standen|title = A history of Standen|website = National Trust|access-date = 2016-03-16}}</ref>

After Beale's death in 1912, Margaret Beale continued to live at Standen. When she died in 1936, their unmarried daughter, Margaret, succeeded her, and after her death in 1947, Standen came into the possession of Helen, their youngest daughter, also unmarried.<ref>[http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/rd/66e8120b-7af1-409b-b2cc-f392f9bba462 The Standen Archives, West Sussex Record Office]</ref> On Helen's death in 1972 the house passed by bequest to the National Trust.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

==Estate and garden==
The estate was formed from three farms which the Beales purchased in 1890. The Beales started planting a {{convert|12|acre|ha|adj=on}} garden almost immediately after they had purchased the land, using the site of an 18th-century garden and [[orchard]].<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/standen-house-and-garden/features/relax-in-the-garden-at-standen|title = Relax in the garden at Standen|website = National Trust|access-date = 2016-03-16}}</ref> In early 1891 trees were planted, a yew hedge established and the kitchen garden begun.

The Beales consulted a London [[landscape gardening|landscape gardener]], G.B. Simpson, who drew up a layout that assumed that the new house would be located on the line of the existing terrace.<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.yeoldesussexpages.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=321&Itemid=658&lang=en|title = Ye Olde Sussex Pages - Standen|website = www.yeoldesussexpages.com|access-date = 2016-03-16}}</ref> However, Webb suggested that it rather be placed further into the hillside. The proposed planting schemes were characterised by strict geometrical layouts of colourful flowerbeds and shrubs. Webb preferred something else, however: a mixture of natural styles combining old-fashioned formality and compartmentalised gardens. Webb also designed a number of elements in the garden.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

The resulting Arts and Crafts garden used local materials for its formal elements, and loose plantings amongst yew hedges, [[Trellis (architecture)|trellis]] and [[pergola]]s, emphasising natural colour schemes and subtle combinations of colour and foliage.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

==Standen Wood==
The National Trust acquired Standen Wood, originally part of the larger estate at the property, in 2001. The wood had been owned and managed as a nature reserve since the 1970s and is a haven for birds.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

'''Uppark''' is a 17th-century house in [[South Harting]], [[West Sussex]], England. It is a Grade I [[listed building]]<ref>{{NHLE|desc=Uppark (National Trust)|num=1025979|access-date=28 May 2017}}</ref> and a [[National Trust]] property.

==History==

The house, set high on the [[South Downs]], was built for [[Ford Grey, 1st Earl of Tankerville]] (1655—1701), ''circa'' 1690; the architect is believed to have been [[William Talman (architect)|William Talman]]. The estate was sold in 1747 to Sir [[Sir Matthew Fetherstonhaugh, 1st Baronet|Matthew Fetherstonhaugh]], and his wife Sarah. Matthew and Sarah redecorated the house extensively from 1750 to 1760 and introduced most of the existing collection of household items displayed today, much of it collected on their [[Grand Tour]] of 1749 to 1751.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

Their only son, Sir [[Henry Fetherstonhaugh]], added to the collection and commissioned [[Humphry Repton]] to add a new pillared [[portico]], dairy and landscaped garden. In the 19th century stables and kitchens were added as separate buildings, connected to the main building by tunnels for servants' use.<ref name="NT">{{cite book|last1=Rowell|first1=Christopher|title=Uppark|date=1995|publisher=National Trust|isbn=0-7078-0198-2}}</ref> Sir Harry married, at the age of 71, the estate's dairymaid, 21-year-old Mary Ann Bullock, to whom he left Uppark on his death in 1846. She in turn, after considerably upgrading the property, left it to her sister Frances on her own death in 1874.  Frances Bullock, under her adopted name of Miss Fetherstonhaugh, was determined to fulfill the trust her sister had passed on. She chose her two friends, Colonel Keith Turnour and Admiral [[Herbert Meade-Fetherstonhaugh|Herbert Meade]], to be her heirs in succession. Both were selected as second sons who could, therefore, adopt her name, which both went on to do.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wyndham |first1=Richard |title=Last Look Round |date=1940 |publisher=Batsford |location=London}}</ref>  

Admiral Meade's wife, Margaret, became the next mistress of Uppark in 1931. She continued caring for the house and contents as the Bullock sisters had done. After [[World War II]], Admiral Meade-Fetherstonhaugh and his son, Richard, entered into negotiations with the National Trust, the outcome being that Uppark passed to the Trust in 1954.  The house is open to the public, except for private apartments leased from the Trust that are still used as a home.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

===Influence on H. G. Wells===
The 20 year-old [[H. G. Wells]] spent the winter of 1887/88 convalescing at Uppark, where his mother, Sarah, was housekeeper between 1880 and 1893.<ref name=Pevsner>{{cite book |last=Nairn |first=Ian |author-link=Ian Nairn |author2=Pevsner, Nikolaus |author-link2=Nikolaus Pevsner  |title=[[Pevsner Architectural Guides#Buildings of England|The Buildings of England]]: Sussex |publisher=[[Penguin Books]] |location=Harmondsworth |year=1965 |isbn=0-14-071028-0 |pages=358–60}}</ref> She had previously been employed there between 1850 and 1855, as housemaid to Lady Fetherstonhaugh's sister, and Wells had paid many visits to her during his boyhood.  Wells' father [[Joseph Wells (cricketer)|Joseph]], a gardener, was employed at Uppark in 1851 and he and Sarah married in 1853.<ref name=Wells>{{cite book |title=H.G. Wells: Experiment in Autobiography |url=https://www.fadedpage.com/showbook.php?pid=20100511 |publisher=J. B. Lippincott Co. |location=New York |year=1934 |first=Herbert G. |last=Wells}}</ref>

The house and the social hierarchy it embodied had an important effect on Wells' outlook. The deep class divisions he observed there helped to inspire many of his meritocratic, liberal and socialist views.<ref>Michael Sherborne, ''H.G. Wells: Another Kind of Life'' (London: 2010), pp. 40-42.</ref> This development was further encouraged by his discovery, in Uppark's large library, of works by philosophers and radicals such as [[Plato]], [[Voltaire]] and [[Thomas Paine]].<ref>Sherborne, ''H.G. Wells'', pp. 50-51.</ref> These impressions were reflected in his later work: for example, the contrast between the sunny and carefree world of the [[Eloi]] and the dark caves of the [[Morlock]]s in ''[[The Time Machine]]'' is commonly regarded to have been inspired by the inequalities Wells observed at Uppark.<ref>Sherborne, ''H.G. Wells'', p. 104.</ref> Also significant was Wells' discovery of a [[telescope]] in the house's attic, which gave the future author of ''[[The War of the Worlds]]'' his first opportunity to examine the night sky in detail.<ref>Wells, ''Experiment in Autobiography'', p. 106</ref>

===Fire===
On 30 August 1989 the building was devastated by a fire caused by a workman's [[blowtorch]] whilst repairing lead flashing on the roof, just two days before the work was due to be completed.<ref name="independent">{{cite news|last1=Glancey|first1=Jonathan|title=High price of keeping up with 'heritage mania': The National Trust is|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/high-price-of-keeping-up-with-heritage-mania-the-national-trust-is-pursuing-a-building-firm-for-up-1453992.html|access-date=12 December 2016|work=The Independent|date=8 April 1993}}</ref> The fire broke out during opening hours. Many works of art and pieces of furniture were carried out of the burning building by members of the Meade-Fetherstonehaugh family, National Trust staff and members of the public. Although the garret and first floors collapsed onto the lower floors and the garret and first-floor contents were lost completely, the floors largely fell clear of the ground-floor walls and much of the panelling and decoration survived.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

Much of the contents of the ground floor were crushed but not burned; metalwork was able to be straightened and cleaned, crystal [[chandelier]]s were able to be reassembled, and even the elaborate tassels on the chandelier ropes were able to be conserved. The decision to restore the house came after it was determined that restoration would be a cheaper insurance settlement than complete payout for a total loss.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

Most of the pictures and furniture in the house were saved. The building has since been completely restored with many lost crafts relearned in the restoration process, and it reopened its doors in 1995.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/uk/restoration-of-mansion-consigns-1991-fire-to-faded-memory-firedamaged-uppark-has-been-recreated-in-meticulous-detail-writes-oliver-gillie-1414771.html|title=Restoration of mansion consigns 1991 fire to faded memory|last=Gillie|first=Oliver|date=19 July 1994|work=[[The Independent]]|access-date=2 June 2012}}</ref> Some "critical markers" remain where visitors can still see the history of the fire, for example many of the floorboards on the principal ground floor retain burn marks.<ref>Musson, J., [https://www.open.edu/openlearn/mod/oucontent/view.php?id=69167&section=4.2 Interview], in ''OpenLearn'', ''Exploring philosophy: faking nature'', Week 3, section 4.2, accessed 17 July 2023</ref>

==Public access==
The house is open to the public four days a week for most of the year other than Christmas.<ref>{{cite web|title=Opening Times (Uppark)|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/place-pages/345/pages/opening-times-calendar|website=National Trust|access-date=28 May 2017}}</ref>

It is near Ardingly, West Sussex in the High Weald (grid reference TQ340315), and comprises a late 16th-century mansion, a mainly 20th-century garden and, in a modern building, Kew's Millennium Seed Bank. Visitors are able to see the gardens and mansion, and also visit the seed bank. The garden today covers some 2 km2 (490 acres) and includes walled and water gardens, woodland and wetland conservation areas.
RBG Kew has leased the land from the National Trust since 1965 and much has been achieved in this time, from the Millennium Seed Bank project and the creation of the Loder Valley and Francis Rose Nature Reserves to the introduction of the visitor centre, the Seed café and Stables restaurant, along with the development of the gardens.
Wakehurst is listed Grade I on the National Heritage List for England, and its gardens are listed Grade II* on the Register of Historic Parks and Gardens.
The stables are listed Grade II* and the South Lodge and gateway is listed Grade II.

'''Kew Wakehurst''', previously known as '''Wakehurst''' and '''Wakehurst Place''', is a house and botanic gardens in [[West Sussex]], England, owned by the [[National Trust]] but used and managed by the [[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] (RBG Kew). It is near [[Ardingly]], West Sussex in the [[Weald|High Weald]] ([[Ordnance Survey National Grid|grid reference]] TQ340315), and comprises a late 16th-century mansion, a mainly 20th-century garden and, in a modern building, Kew's [[Millennium Seed Bank]]. Visitors are able to see the gardens and mansion, and also visit the seed bank. The garden today covers some {{cvt|2|km2|acre}} and includes [[Walled garden|walled]] and [[Water garden|water]] gardens, [[woodland]] and [[wetland]] conservation areas.

RBG Kew has leased the land from the National Trust since 1965 and much has been achieved in this time, from the Millennium Seed Bank project and the creation of the Loder Valley and Francis Rose Nature Reserves to the introduction of the visitor centre, the Seed café and Stables restaurant, along with the development of the gardens.

Wakehurst is [[Listed building#England and Wales|listed Grade I]] on the [[National Heritage List for England]], and its gardens are listed Grade II* on the [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]].<ref name=NHLEhouse>{{NHLE|num=1025764|desc=Wakehurst Place|date=28 October 1957|access-date=11 March 2018|mode=cs2}}</ref><ref name=NHLEpark>{{NHLE|num=1000189|desc=Wakehurst Place|date=1 June 1984|access-date=11 March 2018|mode=cs2}}</ref>

The stables are listed Grade II* and the South Lodge and gateway is listed Grade II.<ref name=NHLElodge>{{NHLE|num=1025765|desc=The South Lodge and Gateway, Wakehurst Place|access-date=11 March 2018|mode=cs2}}</ref><ref name=NHLEstables>{{NHLE|num=1354792|desc=Stables to the north east of Wakehurst Place|date=28 October 1957|access-date=11 March 2018|mode=cs2}}</ref>

==History==
The mansion was built by Sir [[Culpeper baronets|Edward Culpeper]] in 1590. It originally formed a complete courtyard prior to being altered various times, and currently has an E-shaped plan. Wakehurst was bought in 1694 by Dennis Lyddell, [[comptroller]] of the [[Treasurer of the Navy]]'s accounts and briefly MP for [[Harwich (UK Parliament constituency)|Harwich]]. His son [[Richard Liddell]], a profligate [[rake (stock character)|rake]], was discovered in [[criminal conversation]] ([[adultery]]) with Lady Bergavenny, wife of [[William Nevill, 16th Baron Bergavenny]]. Nevill brought a lawsuit against Liddell who, rather than pay the damages of £10,000, handed the Wakehurst estate over to his younger brother Charles and went abroad. He was later an opposition Whig MP for [[Bossiney (UK Parliament constituency)|Bossiney]] in [[Cornwall]], and briefly [[Chief Secretary for Ireland]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.historyofparliamentonline.org/volume/1715-1754/member/liddell-richard-1694-1746 |title=Liddell, Richard (?1694–1746), of Wakehurst Place, Suss. |publisher=History of Parliament Online |access-date=25 June 2014}}</ref>

The house was illustrated in [[Joseph Nash]]'s [https://archive.org/details/cu31924015353471/page/n206/mode/1up?q=wakehurst&view=theater ''The Mansions of England in the Olden Time''] (1839), pp. 97–98.

It was sold in 1869 to Caroline, [[Arthur Hill, 4th Marquess of Downshire|Dowager Marchioness of Downshire]] and then passed to the [[Boord baronets]].<ref>[https://www.british-history.ac.uk/vch/sussex/vol7/pp127-132 'Parishes: Ardingly'], in ''A History of the County of Sussex: Volume 7, the Rape of Lewes'', ed. L. F. Salzman (London, 1940). British History Online. [Retrieved 28 November 2024].</ref>

The gardens were largely created by [[Gerald Loder, 1st Baron Wakehurst|Gerald Loder]] (later Lord Wakehurst) who purchased the estate in 1903 and spent 33 years developing the gardens.<ref>{{cite web |title=Wakehurst Place: The Culpeper Connection |url=http://gen.culpepper.com/archives/uk/places/wakehurst5.htm}}</ref> He was succeeded by Sir [[Henry Price (tailor)|Henry Price]], under whose care the Loder plantings matured. Sir Henry left Wakehurst to the nation in 1963 and the Royal Botanic Gardens took up a lease from the National Trust in 1965. In 1967, Tony Schilling was appointed as Curator of Wakehurst Place where he remained until 1991.<ref name="Armitage2025">{{Cite journal |last=Armitage |first=James |date=2025 |title=Daphne bholua 'Peter Smithers' |journal=The Garden |volume=150 |issue=3 |pages=48}}</ref>

In 1887, American architect [[Dudley Newton]] completed a replica of Wakehurst in [[Newport, Rhode Island]], for sportsman and politician [[James J. Van Alen]] from plans designed by [[Charles Eamer Kempe]]. [[Salve Regina University]] purchased the mansion from the Van Alen family in 1972.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Salve Regina University |author-link=Salve Regina University |title=Campus Buildings: Wakehurst |url=http://www.salve.edu/campus-buildings/wakehurst |access-date=6 July 2016}}</ref>

In 2022, the mansion was closed for an extensive renovation, predicted to last at least two years.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Mansion: Undergoing restoration |url=https://www.kew.org/wakehurst/whats-at-wakehurst/the-mansion |access-date=18 January 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230118114050/https://www.kew.org/wakehurst/whats-at-wakehurst/the-mansion |archive-date=18 January 2023 |url-status=live}}</ref>

==National Collections==
Wakehurst is home to the [[National Plant Collection|National Collections]] of ''[[Betula]]'' (birches), ''[[Hypericum]]'', ''[[Nothofagus]]'' (Southern Hemisphere beeches) and ''[[Skimmia]]''. The [[Great Storm of 1987]] decimated Loder's plantings, toppling 20,000 trees.<ref>''Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, Souvenir Guide'', 4th ed. 2009:81.</ref> Since then, Kew has redesigned the gardens to create a walk through the temperate woodlands of the world.<ref>{{cite web |title=What's in the gardens |url=https://www.kew.org/wakehurst/whats-at-wakehurst |access-date=9 November 2022}}</ref>

==Millennium Seed Bank==
The [[Wellcome Trust]] Millennium Building, which houses an international [[seedbank]] known as the [[Millennium Seed Bank Partnership|Millennium Seed Bank]] (run by Kew, not the National Trust), was opened in 2000. The aim of the Millennium Seed Bank is to collect seeds from all of the UK's native flora and conserve seeds from 25% of the world's flora by 2020, in the hope that this will save species from [[extinction]] in the wild.<ref>{{cite web |title=Royal Botanical Gardens Kew: Seed Collection |url=http://www.kew.org/science-conservation/save-seed-prosper/millennium-seed-bank/index.htm |access-date=17 February 2020}}</ref> This would represent around 75,000 species. By 2025, seeds from almost all UK species that can be stored as seeds were within the seed bank. In addition, seeds of around 40,000 species were stored in the Millennium Seed Bank. This, and its partner organisations had become the world's largest ex-situ plant conservation project.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Millennium Seed Bank {{!}} Kew |url=https://www.kew.org/wakehurst/whats-at-wakehurst/millennium-seed-bank |access-date=2025-06-08 |website=www.kew.org |language=en}}</ref>

Nearby, also cared for by Kew, are the Loder Valley Nature Reserve of woodland, meadowland and wetland habitats, and the Francis Rose Reserve, the first devoted to [[cryptogam]]s (mosses, lichens and ferns).{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

==Christmas tree==
Wakehurst is home to the largest growing [[Christmas tree]] in England, a [[giant redwood]]. The tree stands {{convert|35|m}} tall and is lit with around 1,800 lights from [[Advent]] until [[Twelfth Night (holiday)|Twelfth Night]].<ref name="Christmas">{{cite news |url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/england/southern_counties/4043653.stm |title='Biggest Christmas tree' lit up |work=[[BBC News]] |date=26 November 2004 |access-date=26 June 2014}}</ref> The lightbulbs on the tree were changed in 2006 to energy-saving lightbulbs, so the tree is not as bright as before but uses less energy.{{Citation needed|date=July 2022}}

==In popular culture==
Much of [[Kenneth Branagh]]'s 2006 film ''[[As You Like It (2006 film)|As You Like It]]'', adapted from [[Shakespeare]]'s play, was filmed on location at Wakehurst.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://bufvc.ac.uk/shakespeare/index.php/title/av66497 |title=As You Like It |publisher=[[British Universities Film and Video Council]] |access-date=17 December 2018}}</ref>

On 4 June 2021, the [[BBC]] broadcast an episode of ''[[Gardeners' World]]'' from Wakehurst.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/m000wntx |title=Gardeners' World Episode 12 |publisher=[[British Broadcasting Corporation]] |access-date=4 June 2021}}</ref>

4487799.extract:
Harting is a civil parish in the Chichester District of West Sussex, England. It is situated on the northern flank of the South Downs, around 3.5 miles (5.6 km) southeast of Petersfield in Hampshire. It comprises the village of South Harting and the hamlets of East Harting, West Harting and Nyewood.
The area of the parish is 3,216 hectares (7,950 acres). At the 2011 Census, the population was 1,451, an increase from 1,407 at the 2001 Census.

'''Harting''' is a [[civil parish]] in the [[Chichester District]] of [[West Sussex]], England. It is situated on the northern flank of the [[South Downs]], around {{convert|3.5|miles|km}} southeast of [[Petersfield]] in [[Hampshire]]. It comprises the village of [[South Harting]] and the hamlets of [[East Harting]], [[West Harting]] and [[Nyewood]].

The area of the parish is {{convert|3216|ha|acres}}. At the [[United Kingdom Census 2011|2011 Census]], the population was 1,451, an increase from 1,407 at the [[United Kingdom Census 2001|2001 Census]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.neighbourhood.statistics.gov.uk/dissemination/LeadKeyFigures.do?a=7&b=11124270&c=Harting&d=16&e=15&g=6473726&i=1001x1003x1032x1004&m=0&r=1&s=1493217090524&enc=1 |title=Harting (Parish): Key Figures for 2001 Census |work=Neighbourhood Statistics |publisher=Office for National Statistics |accessdate=26 April 2017 |archive-date=27 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170427005824/http://www.neighbourhood.statistics.gov.uk/dissemination/LeadKeyFigures.do?a=7&b=11124270&c=Harting&d=16&e=15&g=6473726&i=1001x1003x1032x1004&m=0&r=1&s=1493217090524&enc=1 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==History==
Harting was listed in the [[Domesday Book]] (1086) under the ancient [[Hundred (county division)|hundred]] of [[Dumpford]] as the large Manor of ''Hertinges'', which included 196 households encompassing South, West and East Harting.  They were 134 villagers, 42 smallholders and 20 slaves.  With resources including ploughing lands, meadows, woodland and nine mills, it had a value to the lords of the manor of £100. The joint lords were the church of St Nicholas, Arundel, and Earl Roger of Shrewsbury.<ref name="Domesday">{{cite web|title=Open Domesday: (East, South and West) Harting|url=https://opendomesday.org/place/XX0000/east-south-and-west-harting/|accessdate=23 June 2019}}</ref>

Apart from three generations of the Earls Montgomery the manor was in the possession of the Crown until 1610 when it was granted to the Caryll family. In 1746 the manor was purchased by the Featherstonhaugh ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|f|æ|n|ʃ|ɔː}} {{respell|FAN|shaw}}) family, in whose possession it remains.<ref name="GENUKI">{{cite web|title=GENUKI - Harting|url=https://www.genuki.org.uk/big/eng/SSX/Harting/|accessdate=29 September 2014}}</ref>

== Harting Down ==
The villages are overlooked by [[Harting Downs|Harting Down]], a {{convert|550|acre|km2|adj=on}} common owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] and part of the [[Sussex Downs]] [[Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty]]. Rising to {{Convert|229|m}}, it offers panoramic views over the [[Weald]] to the north, to the [[English Channel]] and the [[Isle of Wight]] to the south.

Archaeological evidence has suggested that Harting Down was first occupied around 5000 years ago. Neighbouring [[Beacon Hill, West Sussex|Beacon Hill]] is home to a hillfort from the [[Iron Age]], built around 500 BC as an animal enclosure and refuge. In addition, a [[Cross dyke|cross ridge dyke]] was built around the same time, may have been used to control movement of people and animals along the ridgeway.<ref>[http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-global/w-localtoyou/w-south_east/w-south_east-countryside/w-south_east-places-west_sussex/w-south_east-places-west_sussex-harting_down.htm National Trust - Harting Down]</ref>

Because of its elevation Beacon Hill, just to the east of Harting Down, hosted a station in the [[Semaphore line|shutter telegraph chain]], from 1796 to 1816,  which connected the Admiralty in [[London]] to its naval ships in [[Portsmouth]] and [[Plymouth]]. This was replaced in 1822 by a semaphore station which operated on a slightly different route until 1847. [[Bertrand Russell]] and his wife Dora founded the experimental Beacon Hill School<ref>[http://digitalcommons.mcmaster.ca/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1913&context=russelljournal David Harley ''Beacon Hill School'']</ref> at Telegraph House, which was their residence in 1927.<ref>[http://digitalcommons.mcmaster.ca/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1286&context=russelljournal Kenneth Blackwell and Sheila Turcon ''Russell's Addresses'']</ref>

West of Beacon Hill is Tower hill, on top of which is the [[Vandalian Tower]], a folly dating to the 18th century which is in the grounds of [[Uppark]] house. It was built to celebrate the founding of the American colony of [[Vandalia (colony)|Vandalia]] in 1774, though the events of the [[American Revolution]] meant that the colony never got off the ground. The tower is in ruins and cannot be entered, but can be seen from outside.

A large portion of the down has never been used for modern [[intensive farming]] and is thus an important site representing the [[chalk]] grassland that once covered the downs. Plants found on the site include [[quaking grass]] and the [[common spotted orchid]]. The down supports animals such as [[Vipera berus|adder]]s, [[skylark]]s and several species of [[butterfly]].

==Governance==
An [[Wards and electoral divisions of the United Kingdom|electoral ward]] of the same name covers this parish and the neighbouring parishes of [[Elsted and Treyford]] and [[Trotton with Chithurst]]. The ward's population at the 2011 Census was 2,026.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.neighbourhood.statistics.gov.uk/dissemination/LeadKeyFigures.do?a=7&b=13695013&c=Harting&d=14&e=62&g=6473726&i=1001x1003x1032x1004&m=0&r=1&s=1493220880352&enc=1 |title=Harting (Ward): Key Figures for 2011 Census |work=Neighbourhood Statistics |publisher=Office for National Statistics |accessdate=26 April 2017}}</ref>

6619752.title: Ormesby Hall
6619752.extract:
Ormesby Hall, a Grade I listed building, is a predominantly 18th-century mansion house built in the Palladian style and completed in 1754. It is situated in Ormesby, Middlesbrough, North Yorkshire in the north-east of England.
The home of the Pennyman family, originally dating from c. 1600, the property has been much modernised. Now described as a "classic Georgian mansion", it comprises a main residential block and an adjacent stable block. The stable block housed the horses of Cleveland Police Mounted Section until their disbandment in December 2013.
The Pennyman family began acquiring land in Ormesby in the 16th century and bought the Manor of Ormesby in about 1600 from the Conyers/Strangeways family. They acquired a Baronetcy from Charles II for fighting on the side of the royalists in the English Civil War, which became extinct in 1852 with the death of Sir William Pennyman. They lived in the house until 1983 when the National Trust opened the property and its 270 acres (110 ha) of land to the public after the death of Mrs Ruth Pennyman.
The house contains significant plasterwork, a Victorian kitchen and laundry areas, gardens and estate walks. There is also a model railway which is open to the public.
Ormesby Hall holds a range of events throughout the year.
The historic barn at the estate farm was destroyed by fire in August 2023.

'''Nymans''' is an [[English garden]] to the south of the village of [[Handcross]], and in the [[civil parish]] of [[Slaugham]] in [[West Sussex]], England. The garden was developed, starting in the late nineteenth century, by three generations of the Messel family, and was brought to renown by [[Leonard Messel]].

In 1953 Nymans became a [[National Trust]] property.<ref>[https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/nymans National Trust: Nymans].</ref> Nymans is the origin of many [[sport (botany)|sports]], selections and hybrids, both planned and serendipitous, some of which can be identified by the term ''nymansensis'', "of Nymans". ''[[Eucryphia|Eucryphia × nymansensis]]''  (''E. cordifolia'' × ''E. glutinosa'') is also known as ''E.'' "Nymansay".  ''[[Magnolia × loebneri]]'' 'Leonard Messel', Camellia 'Maud Messel' and ''[[Forsythia suspensa]]'' 'Nymans', with its bronze young stems, are all familiar shrubs to gardeners.

The gardens are listed [[Grade II*]] in [[Historic England]]'s [[Register of Parks and Gardens]],<ref name=NHLE>{{NHLE|num=1000160|desc=Nymans |access-date=9 June 2022}}</ref> and the house is a Grade II [[listed building]].<ref name=NHLE2>{{NHLE|num=1025612|desc=Nymans |access-date=9 June 2022|fewer-links=y}}</ref> During 2025, the gardens received 415,569 visitors.<ref name=ALVA />

==History==
In the late nineteenth century, Ludwig Ernest Wilhelm Leonard Messel (1847–1915), a member of a German Jewish banking family, settled in England and bought the Nymans estate, a house with {{convert|600|acre|ha|0|order=flip}} on a sloping site overlooking the picturesque [[High Weald]] of Sussex. There he set about turning the estate into a place for family life and entertainment, with an [[Arts and Crafts movement|Arts and Crafts]]-inspired garden room where [[topiary]] features contrast with new plants from temperate zones around the world.

After buying the property in 1890, Messel set about transforming the original [[Regency architecture|Regency house]] into a German-style structure. Ludwig's brother [[Alfred Messel]], already a well-known architect in Germany, drew up the plans; construction work was carried out by local builders.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/nymans/features/the-architecture-of-nymans | title=The architecture of Nymans }}</ref>

Messel's head gardener from 1895 was James Comber, whose expertise helped form plant collections at Nymans of [[camellia]]s, [[rhododendron]]s, which unusually at the time were combined with planting [[Erica (plant)|heather]] (''[[Erica (plant)|Erica]]'') [[eucryphia]]s and [[magnolia]]s. [[William Robinson (gardener)|William Robinson]] advised in establishing the Wild Garden.<ref>Garden history of Nymans: Leonard Messel, ''[[A Garden Flora: Trees and Flowers Grown in the Gardens at Nymans]]'', (1918); L. M. H. Parsons 1971 "The gardens at Nymans". ''Journal of the Royal Horticultural Society'' '''96'''.11) (1971: 482-491); A. P. M. Rosse, ''Nymans: The Home of the Earl and Countess of Rosse'', (National Trust, 1973); A. Rosse and A. Buchanan, ''Nymans, West Sussex'' (National Trust, 1990); Shirley Nicholson, ''Nymans: the story of a Sussex garden'' (1992);</ref>

Messel, who was of Jewish ancestry and of German extraction, was harassed during the [[First World War]]. Unsubstantiated rumours abounded that he used the tower at Nymans for the purposes of espionage.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/nymans/features/the-architecture-of-nymans | title=The architecture of Nymans }}</ref>

Ludwig's son Colonel Leonard Messel succeeded to the property in 1915 and, at the request of his wife [[Maud Messel|Maud]], replaced the German-style wood-beam house with a picturesque mock-medieval stone manor, designed by Sir [[Walter Tapper]] and [[Norman Evill]] in a mellow late [[Gothic Revival architecture|Gothic]]/[[Tudor Revival architecture|Tudor style]]. He and Maud (daughter of [[Edward Linley Sambourne]]) extended the garden to the north and subscribed to seed collecting expeditions in the Himalayas and South America.

The garden reached a peak in the 1930s and was regularly opened to the public. The severe reduction of staff in World War II was followed in 1947 by a disastrous fire in the house, which survives as a garden ruin. The house was partially rebuilt and became the home of Leonard Messel's daughter, [[Anne Messel]], and her second husband [[Michael Parsons, 6th Earl of Rosse]]. At Leonard Messel's death in 1953 it was bequeathed to the National Trust with {{convert|275|acre|ha|0|order=flip}} of woodland, one of the first gardens taken on by the Trust. Lady Rosse continued to be garden director.

The garden suffered much damage in the [[Great Storm of 1987]], losing 486 mature trees and many of the shrubs.<ref>[http://www.gardens-to-go.org.uk/Nymans_Garden.htm GardensToGo: Nymans].</ref>  The [[pinetum]], one of the garden's earliest features, was destroyed.<ref>[http://www.touruk.co.uk/gardens/gardenssussex_nymans.htm#text TourUK:Nymans]</ref>

'''Woolbeding House''' is an 18th-century country house in Woolbeding, near Midhurst, West Sussex, England. It is a [[Grade I listed building]].<ref name="historic england">{{NHLE |num=  1221573|desc= Woolbeding House|accessdate= 28 October 2018}}</ref>

It was probably built by [[Sir Richard Mill, 5th Baronet]] between 1711 and 1760 and was originally of a quadrangular plan with an open courtyard in the middle. The courtyard was later roofed over. The house is built of coursed Hythe sandstone in 2 storeys with an attic and has a 7-bay south-facing frontage with 5 hipped dormers. A series of gardens, the '''Woolbeding Gardens''', have been created in the grounds of the estate and they are open to the public.

==History==
The place Woolbeding, meaning "Wulfbeard's people", was recorded in [[Domesday Book]] of 1086, and it had many owners including the de Wolbedinge family and the [[Earl of Arundel|Earls of Arundel]].<ref name="history nt"/>
The manor of Woolbeding belonged to William Aylyng in 1567 and passed by marriage to the Grey family. The Elizabethan building of this period was an H-shaped building. The Greys owned the manor until Margaret Grey married Sir John Mill in 1652, and it was then passed down the Mill family.<ref name="sussex">{{cite web|url=https://www.sussexgardenstrust.org.uk/images/Downloads/Research_Articles/WOOLBEDING%20HOUSE.pdf|title=Woolbeding House: Report on the History of Woolbeding House and Gardens|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181028225604/https://www.sussexgardenstrust.org.uk/images/Downloads/Research_Articles/WOOLBEDING%20HOUSE.pdf |archive-date=28 October 2018 |publisher=Sussex Garden Trust|accessdate=28 October 2018}}</ref> The current house was likely to have been built by Sir Richard Mill between 1711 and 1760 as a quadrangle-shaped building with an open courtyard, although parts of the house including the two chimney breasts and part of walling may be from the earlier building.<ref name="historic england"/> Previous occupants included [[Charlotte Smith (writer)|Charlotte Smith]] and her husband who rented the house in 1785.<ref name="history nt"/>

[[File:Woolbeding Fountain DSC 2006.jpg|thumb|Cedra Fountain]]
In 1791 the Rev. Sir Charles Mill, 8th Baronet sold the house and estate to [[Lord Robert Spencer]], the youngest son of [[Charles Spencer, 3rd Duke of Marlborough]], who immediately made a number of alterations to the house, including the roofing over of the central courtyard.<ref name="historic england"/> The house then descended in the Spencer family via his stepdaughter Diana Bouverie to her daughter, who later bequeathed it to the Lascelles family. They in turn handed it over in the late 1940s to the [[National Trust]], although the family continued to live in the house until 1969.<ref name="sussex"/>

The Woolbeding Estate was leased it to philanthropist and art collector [[Simon Sainsbury]] in 1972, and after his death in 2006, his partner Stewart Grimshaw remained in occupation of the house.<ref name="history nt">{{cite web |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/sussex/woolbeding-gardens/a-history-of-woolbeding-gardens |title=History of Woolbeding Gardens |work=National Trust }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://architecturetoday.co.uk/heatherwick-studio-kinetic-glasshouse-woolbeding-gardens/ |title=Heatherwick Studio creates "kinetic glasshouse" |date=22 November 2022 |work=Architecture Today }}</ref> Sainsbury and Grimshaw started a project to renovate the house and create a series of gardens. The gardens have been open to the public since 2011.<ref name="sussex life">{{cite web |url=https://www.greatbritishlife.co.uk/magazines/sussex/22584980.woolbeding-gardens-near-midhurst-west-sussexs-best-kept-secret/ |title= Woolbeding Gardens near Midhurst: West Sussex's best-kept secret |work=Sussex Life |date=23 May 2016 }}</ref>

== Woolbeding Gardens ==
[[File:Kinetic Glasshouse by Heatherwick Studio seen from Woolbeding Churchyard 18 April 2021 - geograph.org.uk - 6810699.jpg|thumb|The Glasshouse]]
Over the past five decades Simon Sainsbury and his partner Stewart Grimshaw collaborated with renowned designers such as [[Lanning Roper]], [[Julian Bannerman|Julian]] and [[Isabel Bannerman]], Philip Jebb, and more recently, [[Thomas Heatherwick]] to transform Woolbeding Gardens into the horticultural attraction it is today, now open to the public.<ref name="sussex life"/><ref>{{Cite web |title=Visiting Woolbeding Gardens {{!}} West Sussex |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/sussex/woolbeding-gardens/things-to-see-and-do-at-woolbeding-gardens |access-date=2023-04-30 |website=National Trust |language=en}}</ref> 
[[File:Woolbeding. (34541645481).jpg|thumb|Gothic summerhouse at Woolbeding]]
Visitors are greeted by the Entrance Garden, which was transformed from what was once the old farmyard. Julian and Isabel Bannerman redesigned this space to feature a dry garden with formal water pools, surrounded by informal perennials and olive trees. The Bannermans also developed the Pleasure Grounds area as well as The Long Walk; a circular route which features follies that lure visitors around the garden.<ref>{{Cite web |title=History of Woolbeding Gardens│W Sussex |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/sussex/woolbeding-gardens/history-of-woolbeding-gardens |access-date=2023-04-30 |website=National Trust |language=en}}</ref> A lake was created out of a swampy ground across the river. A feature in the gardens is the 11-foot tall Cedra fountain by the artist Walter Pye, which stands on the spot once occupied by a cedar tree.<ref name="sussex life"/><ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.williampye.com/works/cedra |title=Cedra |work=William Pye}}</ref>

The Glasshouse and Silk Route Garden was designed by Heatherwick Studio for Woolbeding Charity, supported by the National Trust.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sfct.org.uk/the-woolbeding-charity/ |title=Woolbeding Charity |work=The Sainsbury Family Charitable Trusts }}</ref> The ten-sided kinetic glasshouse which can open and close, and the surrounding landscaped garden zones showcase 300 species of plants from twelve distinct regions of the [[Silk Road]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.dezeen.com/2022/06/27/heatherwick-studio-unfolding-glasshouse-woolbeding-estate-national-trust/ |title=Heatherwick Studio creates unfolding Glasshouse for National Trust|first=Lizzie |last=Crook |date= 27 June 2022|work=Dezeen }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Woolbeding Gardens glasshouse │West Sussex |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/sussex/woolbeding-gardens/new-contemporary-glasshouse-at-woolbeding-gardens |access-date=2023-04-30 |website=National Trust |language=en}}</ref>

60636383.title: Lavington Common
60636383.extract:
Lavington Common is a 31.2-hectare (77-acre) biological Site of Special Scientific Interest south-west of Petworth in West Sussex. It is a National Trust property.
This site has wet and dry heath, acid grassland and woodland. It has a rich community of invertebrates, especially spiders. Common trees in the woods are silver birch, downy birch and oak, while the shrub layer is dominated by bracken and bramble.
